715.title: Jesus wept
715.hook: at his friend Lazarus's tomb, Jesus weeps (John 11:35)
715.howItsDone: Christians read John 11 in worship and in times of grief, and some point to Jesus's tears as a sign that mourning belongs inside faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was watchmen, who wait for a dawn they can't hurry. Your line was more than watchmen for the morning. Today, from the Psalms to the Gospels, and a tomb in Bethany.

"Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick." That's the whole message. Two sisters, Mary and Martha, send it to Jesus about their brother Lazarus. They don't ask for anything in so many words. A message like that, sent from a sickbed, hardly needs to add the word come. But by the time Jesus reaches their village, Lazarus has already been in the tomb four days.
screen: `HE WHOM THOU LOVEST IS SICK.` → `IT HARDLY NEEDS TO SAY COME.` → `FOUR DAYS IN THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: First, the same sentence, twice. Martha hears he's coming and goes out to meet him on the road. Her first words: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Later Mary comes, falls at his feet, and says the very same words. Two sisters, one sentence. Grief can find one line and say it again. Second, he is troubled. When Jesus sees Mary weeping, and the people who came with her weeping too, John says he "groaned in the spirit, and was troubled." He asks where they've laid him. They say: come and see. Third, two words. Then the verse itself: "Jesus wept." No explanation, no speech. Just tears. And the people standing there say: "Behold how he loved him!" The tears are how they see the love. Fourth, tears before the miracle. Earlier in the same chapter, Jesus told his disciples he was going to wake Lazarus out of sleep. And a few verses after he weeps, he stands at the tomb and calls, "Lazarus, come forth." And Lazarus comes out. So in John's telling, the tears don't come instead of hope; they come right alongside it. Christians read this scene in different ways, and some find in it grief and hope standing at the same graveside. In the story itself, the people standing by read the tears one way: as love.
screen: `THE SAME SENTENCE, TWICE.` · `HE GROANED, AND WAS TROUBLED.` · `TWO WORDS: JESUS WEPT.` · `TEARS BEFORE THE MIRACLE.` · then, large: `JESUS WEPT.`

segments.voice: Let the face soften, forehead, eyes, jaw, and bring to mind a loss: a person, a place, a time of life that's gone. If tears come, let them come; if they don't, that's fine too, just give the sadness room without hurrying it along. If you pray, you can bring the loss there without asking for anything, the way the sisters only said: the one you love is sick.
Jesus wept: at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, in John's Gospel, Jesus weeps, and the people say, behold how he loved him. Today's word.
Your line: behold how he loved him. The tears were how they saw the love. Day seven hundred fifteen.

716.title: Let this cup pass
716.hook: the night before his death, Jesus prays in anguish in the garden (Matthew 26:36–39)
716.carry: not as I will, but as thou wilt
716.howItsDone: Christians read the Gethsemane story especially in Holy Week, and some keep a watch of prayer on the night of Holy Thursday, remembering the request to watch with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Jesus wept: tears the people saw as love. Today, a garden at night, and a prayer with no polish on it.

Supper is over. Matthew says they sang a hymn and went out into the mount of Olives, to a place called Gethsemane. It is night. Jesus tells his disciples to sit and wait while he goes on to pray, and takes three of them further: Peter, and the two sons of Zebedee. To these closest friends he says plainly how it is with him: "My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death: tarry ye here, and watch with me." He just asks them to stay awake with him.
screen: `A HYMN, THEN A GARDEN AT NIGHT.` → `THREE FRIENDS TAKEN FURTHER IN.` → `EXCEEDING SORROWFUL.`

segments.voice: First, flat on his face. Matthew says he went a little further and fell on his face. Down on the ground. The body says it before the words do. Second, the honest ask. Here is the prayer: "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me." Some readers hear an echo of the prophets here, where a cup can stand for a hard portion someone is handed to drink. Jesus asks, plainly, not to have to drink it. He doesn't dress the wish up as something nobler. Third, both halves. The same breath goes on: "nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." The wish isn't taken back to make room for the trust, and the trust doesn't erase the wish. They sit side by side in one sentence. Christians read this line in different ways. Some see in it the full humanity of Jesus, a real will that shrinks from pain. Some see the shape of honest prayer: ask first, then let go. Fourth, friends asleep, and a second prayer. He comes back and finds the three asleep: "What, could ye not watch with me one hour?" Then he goes away and prays again, and then a third time, saying the same words. And the words shift. The second time, Matthew gives them as: "O my Father, if this cup may not pass away from me, except I drink it, thy will be done." The first prayer asked if it be possible. The second already sounds like a man who has heard the answer, and still calls him Father.

segments.voice: Let the hands rest open on your knees and bring to mind something hard that you wish were different. Don't make it noble; find the plain wish underneath, I wish this weren't happening, and say it silently or in a whisper, in your own ordinary words. If you pray, you can offer it just as it is, unpolished, the way it was said in the garden.
Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus prayed to let the cup pass, then added, not as I will, but as thou wilt. Today's word.
Your line: not as I will, but as thou wilt. The wish and the trust, side by side. Day seven hundred sixteen, done.

717.title: Not alone in it
717.hook: Christians see in the cross a God who suffers with humanity
717.howItsDone: Christians meditate on the cross, especially in Holy Week and on Good Friday, as the place where God shares human suffering, and visit the sick and grieving as a work of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Gethsemane, the garden where Jesus asked for the cup to pass. Your line was not as I will, but as thou wilt.
screen: `NOT AS I WILL, BUT AS THOU WILT.`

segments.voice: The garden prayer asked for the cup to pass. In Matthew's telling, it doesn't. Within hours there is an arrest, a trial before the high priest, a night of denials, and then a place called Golgotha. Christian teaching reads the cross in more than one way: some readings ask what it paid for, or what it won. Today's asks something quieter. Who is on that cross, and which side of the pain is he standing on? Watching it from above, or inside it?
screen: `THE CUP DOES NOT PASS.` → `A PLACE CALLED GOLGOTHA.` → `WHICH SIDE OF THE PAIN?`

segments.voice: First, a name. In its first chapter, Matthew's Gospel gives a child the name Emmanuel, and translates it for its readers: "God with us." Not above us, not watching us. With. Second, the cross. Christians read the crucifixion through that name. In their telling, the one hanging there is no stranger to pain, watching from far off. He is inside it: betrayed by a friend, deserted, beaten, mocked. Near the end, Matthew records him crying out the opening line of a psalm: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's the King James wording. Even feeling abandoned, in this reading, is a place he has been. Third, a letter. The Letter to the Hebrews says: "For we have not an high priest which cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities." A double negative, almost shy. It means he can be touched. He knows weakness from the inside. Fourth, how churches say it. Some theologians speak of God himself suffering on the cross. Others hold that the divine nature cannot suffer, and that the Son suffered truly in his human nature. Both keep hold of the same thing: on the cross, Christians say, God came into the worst of human pain, not only above it. The cup is not taken away. In this reading, it is drunk by someone inside suffering, so that nobody in it is alone.
screen: `EMMANUEL: GOD WITH US.` · `INSIDE THE PAIN, NOT WATCHING IT.` · `TOUCHED WITH THE FEELING.` · `CHURCHES SAY IT DIFFERENT WAYS.` · then, large: `NOT ALONE IN IT.`

segments.voice: Picture someone who is suffering right now: a friend, a parent, a neighbor, someone in the news. Breathing in, say their name silently; breathing out, say: not alone, and if the mind starts drafting advice, let the draft go and come back to the name. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
Emmanuel, the name Matthew gives Jesus, meaning God with us, inside suffering and not only above it. Today's word.
Your line: he can be touched. No advice needed, only company. That's day seven hundred seventeen.

718.title: Paul's thorn
718.hook: Paul asks three times for a "thorn in the flesh" to go, and hears: my grace is sufficient
718.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness or long struggle, praying for healing while also praying for grace to bear what stays.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Emmanuel, God with us: the cross read as God inside suffering. Your line was he can be touched.

Paul of Tarsus, the traveling apostle, writes letters to young churches. He has been shipwrecked, he says, beaten, jailed. And in one letter to the church in Corinth, he admits something small and stubborn. There was a thorn. Something in his body, or his life, that hurt and wouldn't leave. He asked God to take it away. He asked again. He asked a third time. Then he tells the answer he got, and it wasn't the one he asked for.
screen: `A TRAVELING APOSTLE.` → `A THORN THAT WOULDN'T LEAVE.` → `HE ASKED THREE TIMES.`

segments.voice: First, the thorn. In the King James Bible, Paul writes that "there was given to me a thorn in the flesh." He never says what it was. Some readers have guessed an illness, trouble with his eyes, or the people who opposed him. The letter keeps its secret, and that silence leaves room: a reader can set their own thorn in its place. Second, the asking. "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." Paul isn't stoic about it. He wants it gone, and says so, like the prayer in the garden two days ago. Third, the answer. "My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays. What changes is where Paul looks for strength: not in being rid of the weakness, but inside it. Grace, in Christian teaching, is God's gift, given and not earned. Here it comes not as a cure, but as enough. Fourth, the turn. A verse later, Paul sums it up: "for when I am weak, then am I strong." It sounds like a riddle. Some Christians read it this way: the weak place is where a person stops pretending to manage alone, and makes room for God's help, and other people's. In this reading, the thorn doesn't make Paul smaller. It makes him someone who can be helped.
screen: `A THORN HE NEVER NAMES.` · `HE ASKED THREE TIMES.` · `MY GRACE IS SUFFICIENT FOR THEE.` · `WHEN I AM WEAK, THEN AM I STRONG.` · then, large: `STRENGTH IN WEAKNESS.`

segments.voice: Name one real weakness of your own, something you can't do well, or can't do alone right now, and notice how you usually handle it: hide it, push through, apologize for it. Then picture one person who could help, see yourself asking, and notice what happens in your chest as you imagine saying yes. If you pray, you can bring the weakness to God the way Paul did.

Your line: strength in weakness. The thorn stayed, and grace was enough. Day seven hundred eighteen, done.

719.title: With hardship, ease
719.hook: with every hardship comes ease, said twice
719.howItsDone: Muslims may recite this chapter in prayer, and some say its line about hardship and ease to one another in difficult times.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Paul's thorn, asked away three times and still there. Your line was strength in weakness.

"But lo! with hardship goeth ease, Lo! with hardship goeth ease." That's Marmaduke Pickthall's English for two short verses of the Quran. Read it slowly and something odd happens. Apart from the 'but' that opens the first, the second line is the same words in the same order. In an essay, you'd cut it. And there it is, said again, the way you'd say something twice to a friend who didn't quite hear you. Or didn't quite believe it.
screen: `WITH HARDSHIP GOETH EASE.` → `SAID AGAIN, ALMOST WORD FOR WORD.` → `WHY SAY IT TWICE?`

segments.voice: First, the chapter. It's one of the short ones near the end of the Quran, called the Expansion, or the Opening Up. Tradition says it came to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, at a hard time. It opens with questions: did God not open up your chest, and lift from you the burden that weighed down your back? Before any promise, it remembers relief that has already come. Second, the small word. Pickthall doesn't write after hardship. He writes with hardship. The ease isn't only waiting at the far end of the road. It walks alongside the hard thing, already in it, even when it's hard to see. Third, the repeat. Some readers hear it as emphasis, the way a person repeats what matters. Some commentators go further: they read the twice-said line as one hardship met by two eases. Either way, the chapter won't say its reassurance only once. Fourth, what comes after. The chapter doesn't end in comfort and a nap. Its closing verses turn to work and to God: when you're free of one task, keep at the next, and turn your longing to your Lord. Ease, in this reading, isn't escape from life. It's what makes it possible to keep going inside it.
screen: `A CHAPTER THAT REMEMBERS RELIEF.` · `WITH, NOT AFTER.` · `SAID TWICE: TWO EASES?` · `THEN, BACK TO WORK.` · then, large: `WITH HARDSHIP, EASE.`

segments.voice: Hold one hardship you're carrying, and let it be there without arguing with it. Then look inside it, not after it, for one small ease that's with you: a person who checks in, a warm meal, a moment when the worry went quiet. Rest on the ease for a few breaths, then the hardship, then the ease again; both are here.
With hardship: the opening of a line the Quran says twice, with hardship goeth ease. With, not after. Today's word.
Your line: it walks alongside. The ease comes with the hardship, not only after it. See you tomorrow.

720.title: Patience in the Quran
720.hook: the Quran praises patient endurance and prayer
720.carry: patience is at the first stroke
720.howItsDone: Muslims speak of sabr as a virtue to practice in hardship, in daily duties and in restraint, and pair it with prayer, as the Quran does.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was with hardship: the Quran's line, said twice, that ease comes with it. Your line was it walks alongside.

A woman is weeping at a grave. A man passing by stops and tells her to fear God and be patient. She snaps at him: leave me alone, you haven't been hit by what hit me. She doesn't know who he is. Later someone tells her: that was the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. She hurries to his door to apologize, and finds no guards there, just the man. And what he says to her, in the hadith collection of al-Bukhari, is one short sentence about when patience counts.
screen: `A WOMAN WEEPING AT A GRAVE.` → `LEAVE ME ALONE.` → `SHE HURRIES TO HIS DOOR.`

segments.voice: First, the word. In Arabic it's sabr. English often says patience, but in one verse of the second chapter, Pickthall reaches for a sturdier word: "O ye who believe! Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Not waiting quietly in a line. Standing your ground while something hard goes on. Second, the pairing. In that verse, sabr comes with prayer. Endurance and turning to God are offered together, as help, not as a test passed on your own strength. And the verse ends with a place to stand: God is with the steadfast. Third, the honesty. Two verses later, the Quran doesn't promise an easy life. People will be tried, it says, with some fear and hunger, with loss of wealth and lives and crops. Then: give good news to the steadfast. Sabr isn't the absence of hardship. It's what someone does in the middle of one. Fourth, back to the grave. The Prophet's answer to the woman, as al-Bukhari records it, is that patience is at the first stroke. Not weeks later, once the worst has passed. At the first blow. It isn't a ban on tears; in another hadith, the Prophet weeps at a death himself. Sabr, in this reading, is the first moment's choice of how to meet what hit you: with tears if they come, but without turning on the person beside you, or on God.
screen: `SABR: STEADFASTNESS.` · `PATIENCE AND PRAYER, TOGETHER.` · `TRIED WITH FEAR AND LOSS.` · `PATIENCE AT THE FIRST STROKE.` · then, large: `ALLAH IS WITH THE STEADFAST.`

segments.voice: Think back to the last small blow you took, a sharp word, bad news, a plan that fell through, and remember its first second: the jolt, the heat, what you said or nearly said. Replay that second slowly and let the feeling be there, and this time take one breath before anything else happens. That breath is a patient moment; rest in it.
Sabr: Arabic, patience, steadfastness. In the Quran it comes with prayer, and God is with the steadfast. Today's word.
Your line: patience is at the first stroke. Tears can come, and the steadfast still stand. Day seven hundred twenty.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sabr, steadfastness, met at the first blow. Your line was patience is at the first stroke.

The phone lights up with a message from a Muslim friend: her grandmother has died. The replies begin with the same Arabic phrase, or its initials: inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un. Different people, different spellings, the same sentence. Muslims say it on hearing of a death, and of other losses too. It isn't a condolence card. It's a verse, and it comes from yesterday's passage.
screen: `A MESSAGE: HER GRANDMOTHER HAS DIED.` → `THE SAME SENTENCE, OVER AND OVER.` → `NOT A CARD. A VERSE.`

segments.voice: First, where it comes from. Yesterday's verses gave good news to the steadfast. The next verse describes them: they are those "Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." That's Pickthall's English. The patient are known by what they say. Second, two halves. We are God's: in this reading, whatever was lost was never simply owned. Not the money, not the health, not even the people we love. Unto Him we are returning: the one who has died has gone back where everyone is going. The sentence holds the loss and the hope in one breath. Third, a widow's story. In the hadith collection of Muslim, Umm Salama tells how the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, taught that someone struck by a loss should say this verse, and ask God for reward in the affliction and something better in its place. When her husband Abu Salama died, she said it, and wondered who could be better than him. Later the Prophet himself asked to marry her. She said it before she could imagine any answer. Fourth, looking back on a week of suffering. Two grieving sisters, and Jesus weeping with them. A wish, said plainly in a garden. The cross, read as company. A thorn that stayed. Ease, promised twice. Patience at the first stroke. And now a sentence for the moment the news arrives. Again and again, the texts give people words for the worst moment, and leave the why unanswered.
screen: `THE STEADFAST ARE KNOWN BY WHAT THEY SAY.` · `WE ARE GOD'S. WE ARE RETURNING.` · `UMM SALAMA SAID IT.` · `A WEEK OF WORDS FOR SUFFERING.` · then, large: `UNTO HIM WE ARE RETURNING.`

segments.voice: Think of something you once called yours and no longer have, a person, a home, a job, the body you had at twenty, and name it silently. Try the verse's shape in your own words, if it fits: where it came from, then where it has gone; or simply, it was given, it is gone, it mattered. If you're Muslim, or if you wish, you can say the verse itself, then let the loss stay a while in the quiet after.
Umm Salama, the widow in the hadith who said this verse on losing her husband, and whom the Prophet later asked to marry. Today's word.
